notes: Annual report of the Board of Park Commissioners for the year ending June 30, 1910, which is largely a history of Golden Gate Park. Curated: Lloyd Lake and its portal, Spreckels and Metson Lakes, the Stadium.

coverage.remaining: Not placed or already on the pages: the Aviary ($6,247 contract, 1890), the Gjoa, the Key Monument and Spreckels Temple of Music (on the pages), the Panhandle lavatory, a marble statue of Eve given by George A. Pope.

findings.description: Clinton E. Worden gave the park the portal of the A. N. Towne residence on California Street Hill, only slightly marred by the great fire, and it was set up on the margin of Lloyd Lake for $765.10; the lake, three acres at 200 feet above tide between Twenty-fourth and Twenty-fifth Avenues, had a footpath around it.

findings.description: Spreckels Lake covered seven acres on the north side of the park between Thirty-first and Thirty-sixth Avenues, 100 feet above tide, with wooded margins and a driveway around it; miniature yachts were sailed there to test the models. Windmills lifted its water from wells near the ocean.

findings.description: Metson Lake, two acres at 185 feet above tide between Twenty-sixth and Thirtieth Avenues in the middle of the park, was filled with water lifted by windmill from wells near the ocean and served, like Spreckels and Lloyd Lakes, as a reservoir.

findings.description: The Stadium, designed by A. B. Spreckels and John McLaren, was an oval of thirty acres east of Thirty-sixth Avenue ringed by a sixty-foot trotting track, with a bicycle track, cinder tracks and room for six football fields inside, a grassy terrace for 60,000 spectators, and tunnels under the track on the north and south; a grandstand then being built would bring the seating to 100,000.
